what-is-react-and-why-use-it: React = a JavaScript library for building screens out of small pieces called components.
You describe what the screen should look like for the current data. React does the updating.
Data flows down from parent to child. Changing data is called state.
Virtual DOM = a light copy of the page in memory. React compares old and new, then changes only the differences in the real page.
React is a library, not a full framework: you add routing, data fetching and so on yourself.
Learn basic HTML, CSS and JavaScript first. The lessons go in order.
set-up-react-with-vite-first-project: Vite = a fast development server and build tool. `npm run dev` starts it.
Create a project with `npm create vite@latest`, then `npm install`.
Browser loads `index.html`, which runs `main.jsx`, which draws `App` into the root div.
Edit and save: Vite updates the page at once, with no full reload.
Scripts in `package.json`: `dev` to work, `build` to make the final files, `preview` to try them.
If something fails, read the error in the terminal first. It usually names the file and line.
jsx-explained-simply: JSX looks like HTML but lives inside JavaScript. The browser cannot read it, so the build tool converts it.
Rule 1: return one parent element (or a fragment `<>...</>`).
Rule 2: close every tag, even `` and ``.
Components start with a capital letter. Styles are objects: `style={{ color: 'red' }}`.
react-components-and-props-explained: A component = a JavaScript function that returns JSX. Its name starts with a capital letter.
Props = the inputs of a component, like function arguments. The parent writes them like HTML attributes.
Destructure to keep it short: `function Greeting({ name, age })`. A default value: `{ label = 'Click me' }`.
Props are read-only. A child never changes its own props.
Text goes in quotes `name="Asha"`. Other values go in braces `age={24}`.
`children` = whatever you put between the opening and closing tags.
Never define a component inside another component.
react-usestate-hook-explained: A normal variable does not make the page redraw. State does.
`const [count, setCount] = useState(0);` gives the current value and a setter.
Calling the setter makes React call your component again with the new value.
Never change state directly. Use the setter, and make a new array or object instead of changing the old one.
State updates are not instant: the variable keeps its old value until the next draw.
Hooks go at the top level of a component, never inside `if`, loops or nested functions.
handling-events-in-react: Pass the function, do not call it: `onClick={handle}` not `onClick={handle()}`.
Need an argument? Wrap it: `onClick={() => remove(id)}`.
The event object `e` gives `e.target.value` for inputs. Use `e.preventDefault()` on form submit.
A child tells its parent by calling a function the parent passed as a prop.
Events bubble up from the child to its parents.
conditional-rendering-in-react: Four ways to show or hide: `if` before the return, ternary `a ? b : c`, `a && b`, or JSX saved in a variable.
A page that loads data has three screens: loading, error, and the data (or an empty message).
Return early for loading and error. It keeps the code flat.
With `&&`, make the left side a real true or false. `0 && ...` shows a 0 on the page.
Removing an element from the page is different from hiding it with CSS.
react-lists-and-keys-explained: `map` turns an array into a list of elements.
Every item needs a `key` that is unique and stable, usually the id from your data.
Never use a random key. Avoid the index when the list can be reordered.
Keys let React know which item is which, so it updates the right ones and keeps their state.
To change a list, make a new array with spread, filter or map. Never change the old one.
Show a friendly message when the list is empty.
react-forms-and-controlled-inputs: Controlled input = its value comes from state: `value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)}`.
State is the single source of truth, so the screen and the data never disagree.
Many fields: one state object and `setForm({ ...form, [name]: value })`.
Checkbox uses `checked` and `e.target.checked`. Select and textarea use `value`.
Validate on submit and show a clear message next to the field.
Clear the form after a good submit by setting the state back to its start value.
styling-react-apps-css-modules-tailwind: Plain CSS file: simple, but class names are global and can clash.
CSS Modules: each class gets a unique name, so styles stay inside one component.
Inline styles: `style={{ ... }}`. Good for values that change, not for everything.
Tailwind: small ready-made classes written straight in the JSX.
Design for phones first, then add rules for bigger screens.
react-useeffect-hook-explained: A side effect = work outside drawing: fetching data, timers, listeners.
React draws first, then runs the effect.
The dependency array decides when it runs: `[]` once, `[id]` when `id` changes, none after every draw.
Cleanup (the function you return) stops what you started: timers, listeners, requests.
In development, Strict Mode runs effects twice on purpose to find missing cleanup.
You might not need an effect: values you can work out while drawing do not need one.
fetch-data-in-react-loading-error-states: Every request has three states: loading, error, success.
Start the request in an effect, and pass an `AbortController` signal.
`fetch` does not throw on 404 or 500. Check `response.ok` yourself.
Cleanup aborts the old request, so old data cannot replace new data (the race condition).
Put repeated fetch code in one helper function.
react-useref-hook-dom-access: `useRef` makes a box with a `current` value that React keeps between draws.
Put `ref={myRef}` on an element and `myRef.current` is the real DOM element after drawing.
Common uses: focus an input, scroll to an element, keep a timer id, remember the previous value.
Changing a ref does not redraw the screen. If the screen must change, use state.
Use refs for things outside the data flow, not as a replacement for state.
lifting-state-up-and-component-compositi: Two components need the same value? Move the state to their closest shared parent.
Data goes down as props. Events go up as functions.
Only one copy of the data, so the parts can never disagree.
Derive values while drawing (like a total) instead of storing a second copy in state.
Passing props through many levels is tiring: use composition with `children`, or context.
Do not lift higher than needed. Keep state close to where it is used.
react-usereducer-hook-explained: `useReducer` is for state with many related changes.
The component sends an action: a small object such as `{ type: 'added', text }`.
`dispatch(action)` hands the current state and the action to the reducer.
The reducer returns a new state. It never changes the old one.
All the rules live in one place, so they are easy to read and test.
react-context-api-usecontext-explained: Context shares data with many components without passing props through every level.
Three steps: `createContext`, a `Provider` near the top with the `value`, and `useContext` where you need it.
Good for theme, signed-in user, language. Not for data that changes many times a second.
When the provider value changes, every component that reads it draws again.
Wrap `useContext` in a custom hook that throws a helpful error if the provider is missing.
Context is not a database. Keep server data in a data library.
react-custom-hooks-reuse-logic: A custom hook = a function whose name starts with `use` and that calls other hooks.
Same state and effect in two places? Move it into a hook, for example `useToggle` or `useLocalStorage`.
Hooks share logic, not data. Each component that calls the hook gets its own state.
Same rules as normal hooks: top level only, and only in components or other hooks.
Good hooks do one job, have a clear name, and return what the caller needs.
Improve the hook once and every component gets the improvement.
react-router-pages-links-navigation: `<Routes>` and `<Route path element>` decide which component shows for which address.
Use `<Link to>` instead of `<a>` so the page does not reload.
A layout route keeps the menu on screen and shows the page in `<Outlet />`.
`useNavigate` moves with code, for example after login.
Protected route = a wrapper that redirects when the user is not signed in. The server must still check.
A `*` route shows a not found page. Static hosts need a fallback to `index.html`.
react-forms-validation-formdata-react-ho: The browser already keeps form values. Give every input a `name`.
On submit: `new FormData(e.currentTarget)` reads all fields at once, so no state per field.
Your own validation function returns an object of errors. Show them next to the fields.
The server must always validate again. Browser checks can be skipped.
React Hook Form helps when a form is large or has many rules.
how-react-renders-rules-of-react-strictm: Render = React calls your component function to get JSX. It is not the same as changing the page.
A re-render starts with a state change, a parent render, or a changed context.
Components must be pure: same props and state give the same JSX. No changing outside values while rendering.
State is a snapshot. Replace objects and arrays, never change them.
Batching: many updates in one event give one render.
React commits only the real differences to the page.
`StrictMode` renders twice in development to help you find mistakes.
react-performance-memo-usememo-usecallba: Measure first with the React DevTools Profiler. Fix only what is really slow.
Simplest fix: move the state down into a small component.
`React.memo` skips a child when its props are the same.
`useMemo` keeps an expensive result. `useCallback` keeps a function steady.
Objects and functions are new on every render, which can break `memo`.
Long lists: show less, or virtualise. Do not search on every key press.
Do not add memo everywhere. It costs memory and makes code harder to read.
react-lazy-suspense-code-splitting: Code splitting = download code only when it is needed, so the first load is smaller.
`const Admin = lazy(() => import('./Admin'))` makes a separate file.
Wrap it in `<Suspense fallback={...}>` to show something while it loads.
Split by route first, then heavy libraries such as editors and charts.
Preload on hover or focus to hide the wait.
Check the result in the build output or the browser Network tab.
react-error-boundaries-portals-modals: An error while rendering can turn the whole page white. An error boundary catches it and shows a fallback.
Boundaries are class components (or a library). They need `getDerivedStateFromError` or `componentDidCatch`.
They do not catch errors in event handlers, fetch, timers or on the server.
Add a retry button and put boundaries around separate parts of the page.
A portal draws a component somewhere else in the DOM: `createPortal(jsx, document.body)`.
A good modal: `role="dialog"`, focus moves in, Escape closes, focus returns.
react-state-management-redux-toolkit-zus: Do you need a library? Only for client state shared by many far-apart components.
Redux flow: a component dispatches an action, the reducer returns new state, components read it with selectors.
Redux Toolkit makes this short with `createSlice`. Zustand does it with one `create` call.
Select only what you need so only those components redraw.
Never change state directly. Keep local state local.
Server data belongs in a data library such as TanStack Query.
tanstack-query-react-data-fetching: Server state is different from client state: it lives elsewhere, can be stale, and is shared.
The query key is the cache key. Include every value the request depends on.
Cached data shows at once. Stale data refreshes in the background.
`useMutation` changes data. Then `invalidateQueries` reloads the list.
Retries, cancelling and caching are built in, so you write less state code.
testing-react-vitest-testing-library: Test what the user sees and does, not the code inside.
Vitest runs the tests. React Testing Library draws the component in a fake browser.
Find elements the way people do: `getByRole`, `getByLabelText`, `getByText`.
`user-event` clicks and types like a real person. Then check with `expect`.
Components that use context or a router need to be wrapped in them in the test.
Good tests let you tidy code without breaking them.
react-accessibility-a11y-guide: Use the right HTML element: a real `button` works with keyboard and screen reader for free.
Label every field. Give meaningful images `alt` text.
Everything must work with the keyboard only. Keep the focus ring visible.
Do not use colour alone. Check contrast.
Use ARIA only when HTML is not enough. Live regions announce changes.
Test with the keyboard, Lighthouse or axe, and a screen reader. Tools find only part of the problems.
react-19-new-features-actions-use-optimi: Actions: pass a function to `<form action={fn}>`. React gives it the `FormData`.
`useActionState` keeps the result, the error and the pending flag.
`useFormStatus` lets a button know the form is sending.
`useOptimistic` shows the expected result at once. If the request fails, it goes back.
`use` can read a promise or context. `ref` is now a normal prop.
React Compiler and Server Components are bigger topics. Check what your tools support before you rely on them.
react-with-typescript-beginners-guide: Describe your data with a `type` or `interface`, such as `User`.
Type props: `function Card({ title }: { title: string })`.
Wrong or missing props show as a red line in the editor.
Types are removed at build time. They cannot check what the server really sends.
Avoid `any`. Read the first line of an error, it is usually the useful one.
react-project-structure-best-practices-d: Organise in clear folders and keep components small, with one job each.
Environment variables with `VITE_` are public. Never put secrets in React code.
Before shipping: test the real build, run Lighthouse, try the keyboard for a minute.
`npm run build` makes the `dist` folder of plain static files. Upload it to a host.
Turn on HTTPS and a fallback to `index.html` for React Router.
Client-only React is weak for SEO. Pages that must rank need server rendering or prerendering.
Next: build projects, then Next.js and a backend.
